00_cold_open: That's a person. And this… is the part of a rocket that just came back from space. Fourteen storeys tall. It falls out of the sky… and lands standing up, on a target in the middle of the ocean. Here's the crazy part. It can't hover. It gets one shot to hit zero speed at exactly zero height. Too early, it flies back up. Too late… it crashes. So how does it do the maths? To answer that, we have to take it apart.
01_giant: Here's the whole Falcon 9: seventy metres tall, just three-point-six-six metres wide. Long and skinny, like a pencil. Today we're opening the bottom part: the first stage, the booster. It does the heavy lifting for the first couple of minutes… then it turns around and comes home. Grid fins near the top. Landing legs at the bottom. Nine engines underneath. Every one of these matters for the landing. But first… what fills the other forty metres?
02_tanks: Almost the whole booster is fuel tank. Two of them. On top: liquid oxygen, chilled so cold it's a liquid. Below it: R-P-one, a highly refined kerosene. They share a single curved wall, a common dome, which saves weight. Together, around four hundred tonnes of propellant. More than nine-tenths of the booster's weight on the pad is stuff it's going to burn. But here's a puzzle. The oxygen is on top, and the engines are at the bottom. So how does it get past the kerosene? Straight through it. A double-walled tube runs right down the middle of the fuel tank. And as the tanks empty, something has to fill the space, or the walls would buckle like a crushed can. That's heated helium, pushing down on the propellant and holding the tanks firm. The walls themselves? Aluminium-lithium alloy, friction-stir welded. Remember how much fuel is in here, because by the time this booster tries to land… almost all of it will be gone.
03_merlin: This is a Merlin. Nine of these push the booster off the ground. And the hard part isn't burning fuel. It's moving it. A turbopump drags oxygen and kerosene in, enormous amounts every second, and rams them into the engine at high pressure. What spins the pump? A small burner of its own: the gas generator. It burns a little fuel just to power the pump, then dumps the exhaust out the side. The fuel and oxygen meet at the injector. The Merlin uses a pintle design, a single central post that sprays them together, a cousin of the engine that landed Apollo astronauts on the Moon. It burns stable even when you turn it way down. Hold on to that. It's about to matter. The hot gas blasts out the nozzle, and the rocket gets pushed the other way. One Merlin: up to eight hundred and fifty-four kilonewtons. That's like lifting eighty-seven tonnes. And it can throttle down, but only so far. Its lowest setting is about four hundred and eighty-two kilonewtons. Not zero. Remember that number. It's the reason this rocket can't hover.
04_nine: Nine engines: eight in a circle, one in the middle. Together, over seven and a half thousand kilonewtons at liftoff. There are no wings or fins to steer on the way up. Instead, the engines themselves swivel a few degrees, pushing the rocket's tail sideways to point the nose. And with nine engines, it can lose one and often still make it to orbit. But going up is the easy part. Coming down, this booster will use only one of them.
05_letting_go: About two and a half minutes after liftoff, the engines shut down. High-pressure helium pops three latches, and pneumatic pushers shove the two stages apart. The second stage carries on to orbit. And the booster… is now a fourteen-storey empty can, coasting at around six times the speed of sound, with almost no fuel left. It has about five minutes to get home.
06_way_home: First, it has to turn around. Little nitrogen thrusters near the top puff gas and flip the booster end over end. Then three engines relight to kill its forward speed, and send it back toward the landing site. That's the boostback burn. Then these unfold: the grid fins. Single pieces of titanium, shaped like a waffle. As air rushes through them, they tilt and steer the booster like a skydiver's hands. Now it's falling back into thicker air, engines first, very fast. To keep from tearing itself apart, it fires three engines again into the wind: the entry burn. A shield of exhaust and a sharp slowdown. But this only works if every part works. In 2018, a hydraulic pump that moves the grid fins stalled. The fins froze… and the booster spun into the ocean, just off the coast. Ours is fine. It's gliding now, steering with its fins, falling at hundreds of metres per second toward a target a few dozen metres wide. And now it has to stop. Using an engine… that can't go low enough to hover.
07a_math: Here's the problem. Remember the Merlin's lowest setting? Four hundred and eighty-two kilonewtons. But an almost-empty booster weighs only around two hundred and fifty. Even one engine, turned all the way down, pushes nearly twice as hard as gravity pulls. So if it slowed to a stop in mid-air… it would start going back up. It can't hold still. It has to hit zero speed at exactly zero height. Engineers call it a hoverslam. The maths is one line from school physics. Speed squared equals two, times the braking, times the distance. Let's plug in an example. Say it's falling at two hundred and fifty metres per second, and braking at twice the force of gravity. It needs about one-point-six kilometres to stop. So the computer lights the engine at almost exactly that height. Not a second early. Not a second late. And here's the twist: as it burns, it gets lighter. Same thrust, less mass, so it brakes harder every second. So the computer re-runs this maths over and over, many times a second, nudging the throttle so both numbers reach zero together. In the last seconds, the legs swing down and lock… and both numbers hit zero, together.
07b_record: It doesn't always work. In 2024, a leg collapsed on touchdown and the booster toppled into the sea. But one booster, B-ten-sixty-seven, has now done this thirty-seven times.
08_outro: So that's how it lands without hovering. One engine. One line of maths. And a computer solving it all the way down. But we only took apart half the rocket. The second stage goes all the way to orbit… and it never comes back. Why not? Tell us in the comments what we should tear down next.
